'''''Trifolium incarnatum''''', known as '''crimson clover'''<ref name="PlantAtlas">{{cite web | title=Crimson Clover ''Trifolium incarnatum'' subsp. ''incarnatum'' L. | website=PlantAtlas | url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.9bw | access-date=2025-08-12}}</ref> is a species of herbaceous [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Fabaceae]]. It is native to Eurasia.

==Description==
This upright [[annual herb]] grows to {{Convert|20-50|cm|4=0}} tall, unbranched or branched only at the base. The [[leaves]] are trifoliate with a long [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]], each leaflet hairy, {{Convert|8–16|mm|frac=8}} across, with a truncated or bilobed apex.

The [[flower]]s are produced throughout the spring and summer, creamy white to rich red or crimson, congested on an elongated spike [[inflorescence]] {{Convert|3–5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} tall and 1.5 cm broad; the individual [[flower]]s are up to 10–13 mm long and have five petals. The banner of each flower does not sit upright, but folds forward.<ref name="Streeter">{{cite book | last=Streeter | first=David | title=Flower Guide | publisher=Collins | publication-place=London | date=2010 | isbn=978-0-00-718389-0 | page=298}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
Two [[subspecies]] are accepted by many authorities,<ref name="WFO">{{cite web |title=''Trifolium incarnatum'' subsp. ''molinerii'' (Hornem.) Syme |url=https://www.worldfloraonline.org/taxon/wfo-0000214188 |website=World Flora Online |access-date=12 August 2025}}</ref><ref name="Euro+Med">{{cite web | title=''Trifolium incarnatum'' | website=Euro+Med-Plantbase | url=https://europlusmed.org/cdm_dataportal/taxon/4621085d-0a33-46ed-a5d1-f275188ec618 | access-date=2025-08-12}}</ref><ref name="EPPO">{{cite web | title=''Trifolium incarnatum'' subsp. ''molinerii'' (TRFIM) | website=EPPO Global Database | date=2013-12-03 | url=https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/TRFIM | access-date=2025-08-12}}</ref><ref name="PlantAtlas2">{{cite web | title=Long-headed Clover ''Trifolium incarnatum'' subsp. ''molinerii'' (Balb. ex Hornem.) Ces. | website=PlantAtlas | url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.24x | access-date=2025-08-12}}</ref> though the [[Plants of the World Online]] database does not currently distinguish them.<ref name="POWO2">{{cite web | title=''Trifolium incarnatum'' subsp. ''molinerii'' (Hornem.) Ces. | website=Plants of the World Online | url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:77315489-1 | access-date=2025-08-12}}</ref>
*'''''Trifolium incarnatum'' subsp. ''incarnatum''''' ('''crimson clover'''). Erect, to 50 cm tall; stem hairs spreading; flowers bright red (crimson), with the petals similar length to the calyx or only slightly longer.<ref name="Streeter"/><ref name="Blamey">{{cite book | last1=Blamey | first1=Marjorie | last2=Grey-Wilson | first2=Christopher | title=The Illustrated Flora of Britain and Northern Europe | publisher=Hodder & Stoughton | publication-place=London | date=1989 | isbn=0-340-40170-2 | page=218 }}</ref> Possibly genuinely native only in southeast Europe;<ref name="Euro+Med"/> a [[Neophyte (botany)|neophyte]] in Britain,<ref name="PlantAtlas"/> and widely cultivated as a crop and fodder plant.
*'''''Trifolium incarnatum'' subsp. ''molinerii''''' <small>(Hornem.) Ces.</small> ('''long-headed clover'''). Smaller, to 20 cm tall or prostrate; stem hairs appressed; flowers creamy white to pale pink, with the petals much longer than the calyx.<ref name="Streeter"/><ref name="Blamey"/> Native in Britain, where it is confined coastal sites in Cornwall, Devon and Jersey as a native plant;<ref name="PlantAtlas2"/> also native in France and the northern Mediterranean region.<ref name="Euro+Med"/><ref name="EPPO"/><ref name="Blamey"/>

== Distribution and habitat ==
The species is native to most of Europe and southwest Asia.<ref name="POWO">{{cite web | title=Trifolium incarnatum L. | website=Plants of the World Online | date=2020-09-02 | url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:523237-1 | access-date=2025-08-12}}</ref>

In mild winter areas, crimson clover typically behaves as a winter annual. The seeds germinate in the first rains of late summer or autumn. The plants grow through the winter, and have a major flush of flowering in late spring. In dry summer climates like the Mediterranean, the plants die after maturing seeds. In sites having sufficient summer moisture, plants can continue growth and flowering; and may even behave as short-lived perennials. The plant uses associations with ''[[Rhizobium]]'' bacteria to fix nitrogen.<ref name="usda">{{Cite web|title=Plant guide for crimson clover (Trifolium incarnatum)|url=https://plants.usda.gov/plantguide/pdf/pg_trin3.pdf|last=Young-Mathews|first=Annie|date=February 2013|website=USDA|access-date=21 May 2019}}</ref>

==Cultivation and uses==
Away from its native areas, crimson clover has been introduced to many other areas, including northwestern Africa, Australia, Chile, India, Japan, Pakistan and the United States. Crimson clover is commonly used in agriculture as a nitrogen-fixing cover crop.<ref name="usda"/> The plant is widely grown as a [[protein]]-rich [[Fodder|forage]] crop for [[cattle]] and other [[livestock]], and is suitable to be made into hay. It is commonly grazed by domestic and wild ruminants.<ref>Heuzé V., Tran G., Maxin G., 2016. Crimson clover (Trifolium incarnatum). Feedipedia, a programme by INRA, CIRAD, AFZ and FAO. https://www.feedipedia.org/node/247 Last updated on 19 April 2016, 11:33</ref> It is often used for roadside [[erosion]] control, as well as beautification, however it can exclude other desirable spring and early-summer species of native vegetation in the area where it is planted. It is sown as quickly as possible after the removal of a grain crop at the rate of 20–22 kg/ha. It is found to succeed better when only the surface of the soil is stirred by the scarifier and harrow than when ploughed. It grows rapidly in spring, and yields an abundant crop of greenery. Only one cutting, however, can be obtained, as it does not shoot again after being mown.

Crimson clover flowers and seedling sprouts are edible, and similar in taste and appearance to [[alfalfa]] sprouts.<ref name="livestrong">{{Cite web|url=https://www.livestrong.com/article/481381-health-benefits-of-clover-sprouts/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110728073028/http://www.livestrong.com/article/481381-health-benefits-of-clover-sprouts/|archive-date=28 July 2011|title=Health Benefits of Clover Sprouts|website=LIVESTRONG.COM|language=en|access-date=2019-02-25}}</ref><ref name="ediblewildfood">{{Cite web|url=http://www.ediblewildfood.com/crimson-clover.aspx|title=Crimson Clover: Pictures, Flowers, Leaves and Identification {{!}} Trifolium incarnatum|website=www.ediblewildfood.com|access-date=2019-02-25}}</ref> They can be added as an ingredient in salads, sandwiches, and other [[dish (food)|dish]]es, made into [[Herbal tea|tisanes]], and can be dried and ground into [[flour]].<ref name="ediblewildfood" /> 100 g of crimson clover sprouts contains 23 calories, 4 g of [[protein]], 2 g of [[dietary fibre|fibre]], and provides 38 percent of the [[Reference Daily Intake|RDI]] of [[vitamin K]], as well as 14 percent of the RDI of [[vitamin C]].<ref name="livestrong"/> It has extremely small amounts of calcium, iron, phosphorus, zinc, selenium and magnesium.<ref name="livestrong"/> Like all sprouts eaten raw, there is a risk of contamination with ''[[Escherichia coli]]'', ''[[Salmonella]]'', ''[[Listeria]]'', and ''[[Bacillus cereus]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.huffingtonpost.com/craig-goldwyn/sprouts-e-coli-risk_b_875103.html|title=Why Raw Sprouts May be the Riskiest Food in Your Grocery Store|last=Meathead|date=2011-06-11|website=Huffington Post|language=en-US|access-date=2019-02-25}}</ref> However, many reputable facilities attempt to regulate and test these crops for such bacteria.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.foodsafety.gov/keep/types/fruits/sprouts.html|title=Sprouts: What You Should Know|last=Foodsafety.gov|website=www.foodsafety.gov|language=en-us|access-date=2019-02-28}}</ref>
